title: The Laffer Curve: Revenue and Incentives
description: Explore how income tax rate changes affect both government revenue and taxpayer behavior. You will map out the relationship between rates and revenue for high earners, estimate behavioral responses using the Elasticity of Taxable Income (ETI), and identify when higher rates actually collect less revenue.
objectives: Compute the static revenue effect of a rate change using IRS data
Apply the ETI to estimate behavioral offsets
Understand when the behavioral offset dominates (revenue-maximizing rate)
Explain why estimates differ across individuals and across ETI assumptions

exercises.title: Static Revenue: 2pp Rate Increase on Top Earners
exercises.prompt:
The top marginal income tax rate applies to income above $400,000. There are roughly 1.8 million filers in this bracket, with average taxable income of about $1.2 million.
Using the static formula:
  ΔRevenue = ΔRate × (Avg_Income − Threshold) × Num_Filers × 10 years

Set the rate change to 2 percentage points (0.02) and estimate the 10-year static revenue gain in billions. Enter your answer below.

parameters.name: rate_change
parameters.label: Rate change (decimal, e.g. 0.02 = 2pp)
parameters.description: Change in the marginal income tax rate

parameters.name: affected_income_threshold
parameters.label: Income threshold ($)
parameters.description: Income level above which the rate applies

hints.text: Start with: ΔRevenue (per year) = ΔRate × (Avg_Income − Threshold) × Num_Filers. For a 2pp increase on $400K+: 0.02 × ($1.2M − $400K) × 1.8M filers. Multiply by 10 for the budget window.
0.02 × $800,000 × 1,800,000 = $28.8 billion per year → ~$288 billion over 10 years. The model uses real IRS data, so your answer may differ slightly.
The model's static score for a 2pp increase on $400K+ income is about −$266B (negative = revenue gain = deficit reduction), so enter roughly −266.

exercises.insight: The static formula shows that revenue scales linearly with the rate change and the taxable income base. With 1.8M filers averaging $800K above the threshold, each percentage point raises ~$14B per year. This is the starting point — before accounting for behavioral responses.

exercises.title: Behavioral Offset: The ETI in Action
exercises.prompt:
Taxpayers respond to higher rates by reducing taxable income: deferring bonuses, increasing retirement contributions, sheltering income through deductions. The Elasticity of Taxable Income (ETI) measures this response.
The standard ETI used by CBO is 0.25. The behavioral offset formula is:
  Offset = −ETI × 0.5 × Static_Revenue

Given your static estimate from Exercise 1, calculate the behavioral offset and the net revenue effect. Enter the final (net) 10-year revenue change.

hints.text: The model's static effect is about −$266B, so the behavioral offset is: −0.25 × 0.5 × −$266B = +$33B (partially offsets the revenue gain). Net = −$266B + $33B ≈ −$232B.
The ETI = 0.25 means each 1% increase in (1−t) reduces taxable income by 0.25%. The 0.5 factor comes from the "log-linearization" approximation at the midpoint of the rate range.

exercises.insight: The ETI shrinks the revenue gain by about 12.5% (= ETI × 0.5 = 0.25 × 0.5). At ETI = 0.25, behavioral responses are relatively modest. If ETI were 1.0 (sometimes claimed for top earners), the offset would be 50%, and the revenue-maximizing rate would be around 70%.

exercises.title: Revenue-Maximizing Rate
exercises.prompt:
Vary the rate change to find the revenue-maximizing top marginal rate. The current top rate is 37%. At what new rate does further increases stop raising revenue? Use ETI = 0.25.
The revenue-maximizing rate formula is: t* = 1 / (1 + ETI × (1/(1-t))) — but use the model to verify empirically by trying several rate levels.
Find the rate change at which the net 10-year revenue is maximized (hint: it is around +35pp to +40pp above the current 37% rate).

hints.text: The revenue-maximizing rate from Diamond-Saez (2011) is t* = 1/(1+a×e) where e is the ETI and a ≈ 1.5 (Pareto parameter for top incomes). With e = 0.25: t* ≈ 1/(1+1.5×0.25) ≈ 73%. So adding ~36pp to 37% = 73%.
At very high rates the behavioral offset equals the static gain, so net revenue approaches zero. Try rate_change = 0.35 (→72%) and 0.40 (→77%) and note that revenue starts falling after the peak.
Due to model linearity, the peak is approximate. The model finds diminishing returns above ~65-70% effective rate. Score around rate_change = 0.33 for the "close enough" validation to pass.

exercises.insight: At ETI = 0.25, the revenue-maximizing top rate is around 70-75% (Diamond-Saez 2011). The US top rate at 37% is well below this peak, meaning there is theoretical room to raise revenue. However, real-world considerations — international mobility, income shifting to corporations, political economy — make the practical peak lower than the theoretical optimum.

exercises.title: ETI Sensitivity and Model Comparison
exercises.prompt:
Conduct a full sensitivity analysis of the Laffer curve for top earners.
1. Compute the 10-year revenue effect at rate changes from −5pp to +30pp
   in 1pp increments, using ETI ∈ {0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.80}.
2. Plot revenue vs. rate for each ETI assumption. 3. Identify the revenue-maximizing rate for each ETI. 4. Compare your estimates to PWBM (Penn Wharton) and Tax Foundation published
   scores for similar top-rate increases.
5. Write a 200-word methodology note explaining why your estimates differ
   from the published scores.

Use the model's batch scoring via: rate_change in np.linspace(-0.05, 0.30, 36)

hints.text: Use Python: from fiscal_model.scoring import FiscalPolicyScorer; scorer = FiscalPolicyScorer(). Loop over rate_changes with scorer.score_policy(policy, dynamic=False).

exercises.insight: Higher ETI flattens and shifts left the revenue curve, lowering the peak and making it more sensitive to rate levels. Real-world ETI estimates range from 0.1 (Chetty 2012 for non-top earners) to 0.5+ (Feldstein 1999 for top earners). The choice of ETI is the single largest driver of divergence across institutional models.
